(1997-09-15) — Whether policy and response cure the omitted route or establish a complete defense; Faragher v. City of Boca Raton (1997-09-08) — Labor and Employment / Supervisory harassment and employer attribution.

### Original Title VII mixed-motive same-decision defense

**Governing question:** Liability under the original Price Waterhouse rule for conduct governed by pre-1991 law.

**Current rule:** Direct decisional evidence, proved by a preponderance, that protected religion was a substantial factor actually relied on shifts the burden to the employer to prove by a preponderance that it would have made the same decision without that consideration. Under the original rule, carrying that burden defeats liability, not merely relief.

**Authority by component:**

- Brown v. Polk County — Part III — The original mixed-motive defense fails on this completed record, 1997-03-17; Part III of the Court's opinion, joined by all eight Associates; Stone-Zsela agrees with resolved liability without joining these same-decision reasons

**Present operation effective:** Brown v. Polk County, 1997-03-17, for the original regime applied to pre-1991 conduct.

**Effective transition:** This entry governs the original rule applicable to pre-1991 conduct; it does not replace the distinct liabilities and remedies of the 1991 Civil Rights Act.

**Exceptions and limits:** The direct-decisional-evidence trigger and actual reliance must be established; no universal burden shift follows from a religious employment dispute. Liability and the lawful calculation and availability of relief remain distinct.

**Holdings navigation:** Brown v. Polk County (1997-03-17) — Labor and Employment / Religious accommodation and completed mixed-motive proof.

### ERISA interference with prospective welfare-plan rights

**Governing question:** Whether welfare benefits outside statutory vesting protection are covered by ERISA §510.

**Current rule:** Section 510 reaches covered discharge or other prohibited conduct undertaken to interfere with attainment of a right the participant may become entitled to under a welfare plan. Nonvesting status is no categorical defense: lawful amendment or termination of plan terms differs from prohibited conduct directed at participants. The claim still requires the applicable participant or beneficiary status, protected plan right, prohibited action, interference purpose, causation and relief authorized through §510's reference to §502.

**Authority by component:**

- Inter-Modal Rail Employees Association v. Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railway Co. — I. Section 510 includes prospective welfare-plan rights, 1997-05-12; Ginsburg, all nine
- Inter-Modal Rail Employees Association v. Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railway Co. — II. The categorical dismissal is vacated for the remaining statutory inquiries, 1997-05-12; eight Associates

**Present operation effective:** Inter-Modal, 1997-05-12.

**Exceptions and limits:** The decision creates no permanent-benefits or general unfair-dismissal rule. Attainment where the participant is already eligible remains unresolved.

**Holdings navigation:** Inter-Modal Rail Employees Association v. Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railway Co. (1997-05-12) — Section 510 includes prospective welfare-plan rights; Inter-Modal Rail Employees Association v. Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railway Co. (1997-05-12) — The categorical dismissal is vacated for the remaining statutory inquiries.

### Independent user additions under maritime economic-loss law

**Governing question:** Whether resale absorbs user-added property into the original manufacturer's product.

**Current rule:** Independent equipment added by an actual initial user after manufacturer delivery retains other-property status when a defect in the original product damages it, notwithstanding resale together with the product. The controlling rule concerns additions that did not cause the casualty. Original manufacture and initial distribution remain integrated; components cannot be separated artificially to create outside-property damage.

**Authority by component:**

- Saratoga Fishing Co. v. J.M. Martinac & Co. — I. Resale does not make independent user additions the manufacturer's product, 1997-06-02; Stevens with Stone-Zsela, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; six

**Present operation effective:** Saratoga Fishing, 1997-06-02.

**Exceptions and limits:** Causal additions, disputed provenance, replacements and mixed user/assembler arrangements remain unresolved. Separate causation, comparative fault, supported loss and valid contractual risk allocations remain necessary; resale alone establishes neither waiver nor recovery.

**Holdings navigation:** Saratoga Fishing Co. v. J. M. Martinac & Co. (1997-06-02) — Maritime Law / Products liability and user-added property.

### Military statement-based conduct inference and evidentiary use

**Governing question:** The §654(b)(2) statement route, construed as a rebuttable conduct-related military personnel inference.

**Current rule:** Under ordinary rational-basis review, a voluntary declaration of homosexual or bisexual identity may be treated as rebuttable evidence of prohibited acts, propensity or intent where propensity means likelihood of acts beyond abstract preference or desire and a genuine rebuttal opportunity exists. The sustained application requires neither a completed act nor individualized operational impairment; it is not a conclusive orientation exclusion. Section 654(b)(2) directs separation after the approved statement finding unless a further approved finding establishes that the member demonstrated no engagement, attempted engagement, propensity or intent to engage in homosexual acts. The First Amendment permits the relevant evidentiary use at that conduct-related scope, without permitting punishment for abstract belief or opposition to the policy.

**Authority by component:**

- Thomasson v. Perry — I. The conduct-related, rebuttable statement inference is constitutional in this application, 1997-06-09; O'Connor with Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas and Breyer; five
- Thomasson v. Perry — II. The First Amendment permits this relevant evidentiary use of the statement, 1997-06-09; the same five

**Present operation effective:** Thomasson, 1997-06-09.

**Exceptions and limits:** Section 654(e) permits omission of processing if the military determines both intent to avoid or terminate service and that separation would not serve its best interest; it does not compel omission. The act and marriage routes have distinct predicates and are not adjudicated here. Denial of meaningful rebuttal, an irrelevant inference, an irrebuttable status exclusion or retaliation for advocacy remains distinct. Service excellence is not an automatic defense, and every identity statement is not an admission of an act. No facial validation, civilian-employment rule, new scrutiny tier or investigation checklist follows; independent due-process, APA, directive-validity and substantive-liberty claims remain undecided.

**Holdings navigation:** Thomasson v. Perry (1997-06-09) — A genuinely rebuttable conduct inference sustains this statement-based separation; Thomasson v. Perry (1997-06-09) — First Amendment / Military statements as relevant evidence.

### Title VII limits on diversity-based selection for layoff

**Governing question:** Whether voluntary affirmative action permits race to select an incumbent for discharge solely to preserve departmental diversity.

**Current rule:** A tie in qualifications and seniority does not remove a race-selected discharge from Title VII. The Weber–Johnson accommodation does not authorize such a nonremedial diversity-only layoff without a connection to a manifest imbalance in a traditionally segregated job category. A qualifying remedial plan need not rest on proof that the employer committed an actionable past violation. Constitutional permission to pursue a diversity interest does not itself supply statutory permission under Title VII.

**Authority by component:**
- Independent statutory permission: Taxman, Piscataway Township Board of Education v. Taxman — I. Statutory permission and constitutional permission remain distinct, O'Connor Part I, all nine, 1997-06-16.
- Remedial connection: Taxman, Piscataway Township Board of Education v. Taxman — II. This nonremedial layoff lies outside the recognized accommodation, O'Connor Parts II–III, joined by Stone-Zsela, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas (five), 1997-06-16.

**Present operation effective:** Taxman, 1997-06-16.

**Exceptions and limits:** This rule neither condemns every remedial layoff plan nor decides the separate constitutional question of faculty diversity. The independent unnecessary-burden holding rests on the particular loss, missing remedial limiting goal and available nonracial tie procedure; it is not a categorical prohibition on every preference that burdens another employee.

**Holdings navigation:** Piscataway Township Board of Education v. Taxman (1997-06-16) — Labor and Employment / Voluntary affirmative action and layoffs.

### Independent medical-monitoring damages under FELA

**Governing question:** Whether asymptomatic negligent asbestos exposure supports independent lump-sum medical-monitoring damages.

**Current rule:** Negligent exposure, increased future disease risk and recommended surveillance in an asymptomatic record do not establish entitlement to independent, unqualified lump-sum monitoring damages under FELA. Those damages cannot be appended to an emotional-distress claim that fails its separate injury threshold. The requirement of injury remains distinct from negligence and relaxed causation.

**Authority by component:**
- Boundary of the damages category: Metro-North v. Buckley, Metro-North Commuter Railroad Co. v. Buckley — II. FELA does not authorize the independent, unqualified monitoring damages recognized below, Thomas with O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Breyer (six), 1997-06-23.

**Present operation effective:** Metro-North v. Buckley, 1997-06-23.

**Open question:** Carefully limited monitoring programs, reimbursement of actual necessary costs, later illness and materially different records remain undecided; no universal bar on every monitoring arrangement is adopted.

**Holdings navigation:** Metro-North Commuter Railroad Co. v. Buckley (1997-06-23) — II. FELA does not authorize the independent, unqualified monitoring damages recognized below.

### Withdrawal-liability collection accrual and installments

**Governing question:** When a withdrawal-liability collection claim accrues under §1451(f).

**Current rule:** Withdrawal creates liability but collection accrues only after assessment, scheduling and demand when a due installment is not paid. Section 1451(f) allows the longer of six years after accrual or three years after actual or constructive knowledge of the cause; fraud or concealment permits suit within six years after discovery. Each missed installment has its own period. A legally effective election to accelerate starts the period for accelerated debt, but a later aggregate demand does not revive already barred installments.

**Authority by component:**

- Collection accrual; separate installments and effective acceleration: Bay Area Laundry and Dry Cleaning Pension Trust Fund v. Ferbar Corp. of California, 1997-12-15; Breyer Parts I–II for all nine Justices.

**Present operation effective:** 1997-12-15.

**Sequence or decisionmaker:** The plan must assess and demand payment as soon as practicable. Payments begin no later than sixty days after demand notwithstanding review or appeal. Payment default requires failure to cure within sixty days after written notice; another plan-defined default must indicate substantial likelihood of inability to pay. Default alone is not an election to accelerate.

**Open question:** Whether a complaint’s alternative full-debt demand itself effects acceleration remains unresolved.

**Related current rules:** Withdrawal-liability installment assumptions and separate collection triggers governs computation and payment; those computational assumptions do not establish collection accrual.

**Holdings navigation:** Bay Area Laundry and Dry Cleaning Pension Trust Fund v. Ferbar Corp. of California — Pension withdrawal-liability collection and limitations.

### Knowing false denials in federal employee discipline

**Governing question:** Whether due process or the CSRA immunizes knowing factual falsification when answering misconduct charges.

**Current rule:** The meaningful opportunity to answer does not immunize an otherwise punishable knowingly false factual denial. The agency must prove the actual falsification and culpability under governing employment rules; losing the underlying dispute, honest mistake, uncertain recollection, legal disagreement and procedural nonadmission are not themselves knowing lies. Otherwise lawful consideration of proved falsity for penalty or credibility is permitted, not mandatory. Sections 7513 and 7701 preserve the actual cause, service-efficiency, process, proof and review requirements rather than establish denial immunity.

**Authority by component:**

- Meaningful answer without denial immunity; conditional penalty and credibility use: LaChance v. Erickson / LaChance v. McManus, 1998-01-21; Souter Part I for all nine; Parts II–III for all eight Associates, with Stone-Zsela additionally joining Part III’s penalty and actual-proof/lawful-procedure qualifications.

**Present operation effective:** 1998-01-21.

**Burdens and proof:** Ordinary misconduct requires preponderance proof under §7701(c); specified performance and senior-executive matters retain their separate substantial-evidence rule. Harmful procedural error, prohibited personnel practices or legal invalidity prevent sustaining otherwise supported action. No criminal burden, jury, different-source corroboration requirement or universal materiality element is added.

**Sequence or decisionmaker:** Section 7513 ordinarily requires thirty days’ advance notice of specific reasons, except on reasonable cause to believe an imprisonable crime was committed; at least seven days to answer orally and in writing with documents or affidavits; representation; and a timely written reasoned decision. Agency hearing permission under §7513(c) is distinct from Board hearing and appeal rights. Required records remain available on request. Section 7703 review is distinct from agency proof, with designated discrimination facts receiving their own de novo treatment.

**Exceptions and limits:** Genuine compelled-incrimination claims and protection against mandatory waiver remain separate. The applicable reporting duty must satisfy its actual authorization and nondisclosure exceptions; no general duty to confess follows. Garrity’s criminal-use protection and Gardner’s official-duty/no-waiver distinction remain intact.

**Holdings navigation:** LaChance v. Erickson; LaChance v. McManus — False denials in federal employment discipline.

### Objective doubt before polling an incumbent union

**Governing question:** The prerequisite for an employer’s safeguarded poll of an incumbent union.

**Current rule:** The Board may require good-faith reasonable doubt of majority support based on objective considerations before a safeguarded poll. The same prerequisite for polling, withdrawal of recognition and requesting a Board election is not inherently irrational. Doubt means objective uncertainty rather than proof of actual minority; cumulative circumstantial evidence may suffice without a counted majority’s direct repudiations. Safeguards do not replace the prerequisite, and the permissible policy is not compulsory for every future Board.

**Authority by component:**

- Permissible reasonable-doubt polling threshold; actual doubt rather than minority proof: Allentown Mack Sales & Service, Inc. v. NLRB, 1998-01-26; Scalia Part II with Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; Parts III–IV with Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Kennedy and Thomas.

**Present operation effective:** 1998-01-26.

**Exceptions and limits:** Polling safeguards remain a truth-testing purpose communicated to employees, assurances against reprisal, a secret ballot, no unfair labor practices or coercive atmosphere, and advance time-and-place notice. Lawful certification and contract protections and statutory representation routes remain separate. No unconditional right to poll, headcount threshold or independent First Amendment rule is adopted.

**Related current rules:** Incumbent-union doubt before acceptance of a bargaining offer governs the distinct accepted-offer cutoff.

**Holdings navigation:** Allentown Mack Sales & Service, Inc. v. NLRB — Incumbent-union polling and agency evidentiary standards.

### ADEA waiver safeguards despite retention of consideration

**Governing question:** Whether retaining consideration or failing to tender it back bars an ADEA claim under a deficient waiver.

**Current rule:** A waiver failing applicable §626(f) minimum conditions cannot bar an ADEA action through retention-based ratification, prior tender or estoppel accomplishing the same bar. The party asserting validity must prove a knowing and voluntary waiver under the applicable statutory paragraph; signature, consultation and later awareness do not replace missing statutory safeguards. For an ordinary individual waiver the safeguards include understandable writing, a specific ADEA reference, no waiver of future claims, additional consideration, written advice to consult an attorney, at least twenty-one days to consider and seven days to revoke after execution.

**Authority by component:**

- Deficient waiver cannot be enforced through retention or prior tender: Oubre v. Entergy Operations, Inc., 1998-01-26; O’Connor with Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer.

**Present operation effective:** 1998-01-26.

**Exceptions and limits:** Applicable group-program forty-five-day and disclosure requirements remain distinct. Settlement of an already filed charge or action under paragraph (2) requires paragraph (1)(A)–(E) and a reasonable consideration period. Compliant waivers remain possible; distinct fraud, contract or equitable claims, other released rights, restitution, recoupment and setoff remain unresolved. No automatic repayment or deduction follows, and the employee must prove discrimination. EEOC enforcement and participation protection under §626(f)(4) remains independent.

**Holdings navigation:** Oubre v. Entergy Operations, Inc. — Age-discrimination waivers and tender.

### Actual violation controversies under LMRA §301

**Governing question:** When does a dispute about a labor contract’s validity fall within §301(a)?

**Current rule:** Section 301(a) authorizes suits for violation of covered contracts, not every formation or validity dispute. A standalone formation-fraud action alleging no violation and presenting no actual or threatened violation controversy does not satisfy that jurisdictional gateway. Validity may be decided when necessary to a properly brought violation dispute; a declaratory action must independently establish the applicable jurisdictional and controversy requirements.

**Authority by component:**

- Violation gateway, validity-defense distinction and bounded declaratory route: Textron Lycoming Reciprocating Engine Division v. United Automobile Workers — Contract validity alone does not establish a suit for violation, 1998-05-18.

**Present operation effective:** Textron Lycoming v. United Automobile Workers, 1998-05-18.

**Related current rules:** Member enforcement of interunion contracts under §301 permits a qualifying beneficiary to enforce a covered contract but does not eliminate the violation predicate.

**Exceptions and limits:** No broad §1331 or federal-common-law jurisdiction ruling follows. Fraud, breach, validity, labor-board and State-remedy merits retain their own requirements.

**Holdings navigation:** Textron Lycoming Reciprocating Engine Division v. United Automobile Workers — Labor-contract violation jurisdiction.

### Preexisting other coverage and COBRA continuation

**Governing question:** Whether coverage existing before election permits denial or termination of COBRA continuation.

**Current rule:** The applicable 29 U.S.C. §1162(2)(D)(i) permits termination on this branch only when, after election, the beneficiary first becomes covered as an employee or otherwise under another group plan containing no exclusion or limitation concerning any preexisting condition of that beneficiary. Coverage already in force before election, continued coverage or a change in its primacy is not that event.

**Authority by component:**

- Existing other coverage is not a post-election event: Geissal v. Moore Medical Corp. — controlling Holdings, 1998-06-08.

**Present operation effective:** 1998-06-08.

**Exceptions and limits:** All independent eligibility, payment and continuation requirements remain applicable; the rule awards no duplicative benefits or substantive coverage beyond the governing plan and statute.

**Holdings navigation:** Geissal v. Moore Medical Corp. — COBRA continuation and other group coverage.

### Independent EEOC enforcement under the ADEA

**Governing question:** Whether affected employees can prevent an EEOC age-discrimination enforcement action.

**Current rule:** Under §626(b), the EEOC may enforce the ADEA without an affected individual’s charge, consent or request for recovery. Section 626(f)(4) preserves that public authority despite a private waiver, even a valid one. Before suit the Commission must attempt informal conciliation, conference and persuasion, but need not repeat an unproductive offer indefinitely.

**Authority by component:**

- Johnson & Higgins Holding 1: independent enforcement, waiver and actual conciliation: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Johnson & Higgins, Inc. — controlling Holdings, 1998-09-21.

**Present operation effective:** 1998-09-21.

**Exceptions and limits:** Public enforcement authority does not dispense with statutory coverage, liability elements or the basis for the particular remedy.

**Holdings navigation:** Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Johnson & Higgins, Inc. — ADEA enforcement, working owners and compulsory retirement.

### ADEA employee status of corporate owner-directors

**Governing question:** Whether corporate ownership or board membership excludes an otherwise employed person from ADEA coverage.

**Current rule:** Section 630(f)’s circular definition invokes ordinary common-law agency and requires evaluation of all relevant incidents of the actual relationship. Corporate form, an employee label, directorship, ownership, profit-based pay or an exclusive three-factor formula alone cannot decide status. Genuine proprietors remain outside employee coverage, while actual employment may coexist with ownership and governance.

**Authority by component:**

- Johnson & Higgins Holding 2: complete-relationship common-law inquiry: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Johnson & Higgins, Inc. — controlling Holdings, 1998-09-21.

**Present operation effective:** 1998-09-21.

**Exceptions and limits:** Covered employment does not itself guarantee board tenure, ownership rights or any particular compensation.

**Holdings navigation:** Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Johnson & Higgins, Inc. — ADEA enforcement, working owners and compulsory retirement.

### Express age conditions and the executive-retirement exception

**Governing question:** Whether business succession concerns or executive rank justify an express age-based retirement requirement.

**Current rule:** A reasonable business purpose for selecting an express age condition does not make the decision based on a factor other than age under §623(f)(1). Section 631(c) permits compulsory retirement only for an employee who has attained age 65, following bona fide executive or high-policymaking employment throughout the two immediately preceding years, with an immediate nonforfeitable aggregate annual retirement benefit of at least $44,000 from the employer’s pension, profit-sharing, savings or deferred-compensation plans, or their combination. Executive status alone is insufficient.

**Authority by component:**

- Johnson & Higgins Holdings 4–5: age versus other factors and every executive-exception condition: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Johnson & Higgins, Inc. — controlling Holdings, 1998-09-21.

**Present operation effective:** 1998-09-21.

**Exceptions and limits:** Employee coverage and the exception’s complete predicates must independently be established; a governance label cannot substitute for either.

**Controlling construction:** Benefits in another form or involving employee/rollover contributions must receive the prescribed adjustment to a straight-life annuity without ancillary benefits under a plan without employee or rollover contributions.

**Holdings navigation:** Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Johnson & Higgins, Inc. — ADEA enforcement, working owners and compulsory retirement.

### FCA retaliation before or without a successful qui tam action

**Governing question:** Protection of employee investigation or assistance under the then-operative §3730(h).

**Current rule:** Section 3730(h) protects an employee from covered employment retaliation because of lawful acts in furtherance of an FCA action, including qualifying investigation or assistance before filing. The employee must establish protected activity, employer knowledge and causation; protection does not depend solely on successful qui tam recovery or surviving the public-disclosure bar.

**Authority by component:**

- McKenzie Holding 3: independent retaliation conditions: United States ex rel. McKenzie v. BellSouth Telecommunications, Inc. — controlling Holdings, 1998-09-28.

**Present operation effective:** 1998-09-28.

**Exceptions and limits:** Ordinary employment complaints do not become protected solely by their label; ultimate liability and remedies require the applicable statutory proof. The employer need not hear the exact FCA label when the facts convey that the activity concerns contemplated federal enforcement.

**Holdings navigation:** United States ex rel. McKenzie v. BellSouth Telecommunications, Inc. — False Claims Act public disclosure and original-source jurisdiction; United States ex rel. McKenzie v. BellSouth Telecommunications, Inc. — False Claims Act retaliation and independent protected activity.

### Union-security wording and independent fair-representation claims

**Governing question:** Whether use of statutory membership language or a standalone NLRA timing objection establishes a judicial fair-representation claim.

**Current rule:** Negotiating a union-security clause in §8(a)(3)’s statutory membership terms does not alone breach fair representation. The established restrictions on compulsory financial obligations remain, and arbitrariness, discrimination or bad faith requires its own operative support; under arbitrariness, the negotiated choice must fall outside the broad range of reasonableness under the relevant facts and law. Statutory wording does not authorize compelled full membership, misleading notice, nonchargeable collections or unlawful enforcement. A claim alleging only that a grace-period arrangement violates the NLRA belongs initially to the NLRB. A federal court may decide a statutory question necessary to an independently supported fair-representation claim; relabeling statutory inconsistency supplies no independent judicial basis.

**Authority by component:**

- Wording, fair-representation standards and Board/court allocation: Canonical Decision Record `marquez_v_screen_actors_guild_merits_1998-11-03.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / 1. Statutory membership wording does not alone breach fair representation; 2. A standalone statutory timing claim belongs initially to the Board, 1998-11-03; unanimous opinion.

**Present operation effective:** 1998-11-03.

**Open question:** Whether a thirty-day grace period restarts after a break, how prior employment counts and whether a particular notice or enforcement practice is lawful remain separate questions.

**Holdings navigation:** [Marquez v. Screen Actors Guild, Inc. — Statutory membership wording does not alone breach fair representation](HOLDINGS.md#statutory-membership-wording-does-not-alone-breach-fair-representation-1); [Marquez v. Screen Actors Guild, Inc. — A standalone statutory timing claim belongs initially to the Board](HOLDINGS.md#a-standalone-statutory-timing-claim-belongs-initially-to-the-board).

### Warsaw Convention exclusivity within the Article 17 field

**Governing question:** Whether local damages law can avoid unsatisfied Convention conditions for a covered passenger injury occurrence.

**Current rule:** When a passenger’s personal-injury occurrence lies within Article 17’s temporal and substantive field, Article 24 subjects the carrier action, whatever its legal foundation, to the Convention’s conditions and limits. Failure to satisfy the accident or bodily-injury condition does not itself remove the occurrence from that field or allow an independent local damages action. Domestic law may identify compensable losses and beneficiaries subject to treaty conditions; it cannot create liability simply because a treaty condition fails.

**Authority by component:**

- Field-based exclusivity and distinction between conditions and coverage: Canonical Decision Record `el_al_israel_airlines_v_tseng_merits_1999-01-12.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / Part I — Local law cannot avoid the Convention’s conditions within its covered field, 1999-01-12; eight direct joins.
- Intentional touching alone does not establish Article 25 willful misconduct: the same Record, Public Projection / Holdings / Part II — The Article 25 argument does not change the result on this record, 1999-01-12; O'Connor with Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer, seven direct Associate joins. Stone-Zsela does not join Part II.

**Present operation effective:** 1999-01-12.

**Exceptions and limits:** Events outside covered embarking, carriage or disembarking remain outside this rule. Article 25’s full operation when willful misconduct is proved remains open; intentional touching alone does not establish that predicate. No categorical rule about every physical manifestation of emotional injury or every intentional accident is adopted.

**Holdings navigation:** [El Al Israel Airlines, Ltd. v. Tsui Yuan Tseng — Part I — Local law cannot avoid the Convention's conditions within its covered field](HOLDINGS.md#part-i--local-law-cannot-avoid-the-conventions-conditions-within-its-covered-field-1); [El Al Israel Airlines, Ltd. v. Tsui Yuan Tseng — Part II — The Article 25 argument does not change the result on this record](HOLDINGS.md#part-ii--the-article-25-argument-does-not-change-the-result-on-this-record).

### Defined-benefit surplus and statutory termination

**Governing question:** Participants’ rights in an overfunded defined-benefit plan and the trigger for termination distribution.

**Current rule:** Participants retain promised and statutorily protected accrued benefits, including the employee-contribution floor, but do not presently own individual shares of all actuarial surplus. Mandatory-contribution protection under §§203(a)(1) and 204(c) uses accumulated contributions with the enacted interest treatment and an annual benefit beginning at normal retirement age, with actuarial equivalence for a different form; voluntary contributions retain §204(c)(4)’s distinct treatment. Lawful benefit payments reducing no protected benefit do not themselves establish forfeiture or cutback.

Closing a contributory benefit structure to new entrants while the plan and obligations continue does not itself trigger §4044 termination distribution. A common-law wasting-trust characterization cannot replace §§4041–4042’s statutory termination process. When termination distribution lawfully occurs, plan liabilities and statutory allocation priorities remain, including employee-derived residual protection; employer reversion additionally requires satisfied liabilities, consistency with law and plan authorization, subject to the enacted timing and employee-residual protections.

**Authority by component:**

- Accrued-benefit protection without individual surplus ownership and statutory nontermination: Canonical Decision Record `hughes_aircraft_co_v_jacobson_merits_1999-01-25.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / III. Accrued benefits are protected without individual ownership of all surplus; IV. Continuing benefit obligations do not trigger termination distribution, 1999-01-25; nine direct joins to the common holdings, eight to the statutory contribution and distribution explanations.

**Present operation effective:** 1999-01-25.

**Exceptions and limits:** No actual benefit amount, reversion entitlement or general rule for every partial termination follows. A fair-administration clause alone does not promise a later incentive to persons outside its lawful eligibility class or authorize judicial redesign; a due benefit, unequal administration among eligible participants or independent statutory restriction retains its own claim. Authority: the same Record, Holding VI, eight direct joins.

**Holdings navigation:** [Hughes Aircraft Co. v. Jacobson — III. Accrued benefits are protected without individual ownership of all surplus](HOLDINGS.md#iii-accrued-benefits-are-protected-without-individual-ownership-of-all-surplus); [Hughes Aircraft Co. v. Jacobson — IV. Continuing benefit obligations do not trigger termination distribution](HOLDINGS.md#iv-continuing-benefit-obligations-do-not-trigger-termination-distribution).

### Assigned school productions and teachers’ personal speech

**Governing question:** Whether a teacher has a personal First Amendment right over an assigned school instructional production.

**Current rule:** Selection, production and direction of material as part of an assigned public-school instructional program are institutional curricular expression subject to the school system’s lawful control. Delegated artistic discretion, public controversy and prior approval do not themselves give the teacher a personal constitutional right against curricular and related employment control or make approval an irrevocable constitutional delegation. A protected personal interest must be established before justification and same-decision rules apply.

**Authority by component:**

- Confined instructional-expression classification and antecedent personal-interest requirement: Canonical Decision Record `boring_v_buncombe_county_board_of_education_merits_1999-02-17.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / Assigned instructional production and the asserted personal speech right, 1999-02-17; five direct joins.

**Present operation effective:** 1999-02-17.

**Exceptions and limits:** Separate citizen speech, independently forbidden classifications or exclusions, and statutory, contractual, tenure and state-law limits remain. This is not a rule for every duty-related statement or university academic freedom, and a curricular label does not establish an actually lawful motive.

**Holdings navigation:** [Boring v. Buncombe County Board of Education — Assigned instructional production and the asserted personal speech right](HOLDINGS.md#assigned-instructional-production-and-the-asserted-personal-speech-right-1).

### Bounded FLRA choice over midterm bargaining

**Governing question:** The federal labor statute’s allocation of authority over union-initiated bargaining during an existing agreement.

**Current rule:** The statute neither categorically prohibits union-initiated midterm bargaining nor unambiguously requires one comprehensive midterm regime. The FLRA may determine timing and extent through a reasonable, explained construction subject to contract coverage, lawful waiver, negotiable-subject restrictions, management rights and federal-law consistency. Section 7106(b)(1)’s agency-election condition is not automatically a condition in (b)(2) or (3). Efficiency and impasse provisions inform administration without establishing perpetual negotiation or inevitable clause imposition. Absence of an independently compelled statutory entitlement does not itself make a contractual midterm proposal unlawful; the actual clause and the agency’s reasons must be examined under the permissible framework.

**Authority by component:**

- Genuine bounded discretion and separate contractual negotiability: Canonical Decision Record `nffe_and_flra_v_interior_merits_1999-03-03.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / 1. The statute leaves the extent of midterm bargaining to bounded Authority construction; 2. Contractual negotiability requires reconsideration under the corrected legal framework, 1999-03-03; six direct joins.

**Present operation effective:** 1999-03-03.

**Exceptions and limits:** No compulsory agreement, concession or Panel award is supplied. Agreed waiver, bargaining over a waiver clause and compulsory acceptance at impasse are distinct; no comprehensive employer-imposed waiver is presumed. Statutory silence alone does not satisfy §§7103(a)(14)(C) and 7117(a).

**Holdings navigation:** [National Federation of Federal Employees, Local 1309 v. Department of the Interior / Federal Labor Relations Authority v. Department of the Interior — 1. The statute leaves the extent of midterm bargaining to bounded Authority construction](HOLDINGS.md#1-the-statute-leaves-the-extent-of-midterm-bargaining-to-bounded-authority-construction-1); [National Federation of Federal Employees, Local 1309 v. Department of the Interior / Federal Labor Relations Authority v. Department of the Interior — 2. Contractual negotiability requires reconsideration under the corrected legal framework](HOLDINGS.md#2-contractual-negotiability-requires-reconsideration-under-the-corrected-legal-framework).

### SSDI representations in ADA qualification proof

**Governing question:** How an earlier total-disability representation affects an ADA employment plaintiff’s qualification showing.

**Current rule:** Applying for or receiving SSDI neither automatically estops an ADA plaintiff nor creates a special adverse presumption. ADA qualification asks whether the person can perform essential job functions with or without reasonable accommodation, a different inquiry from SSDI. A plaintiff confronting an apparently inconsistent earlier total-disability representation must explain it sufficiently for a reasonable juror, accepting the earlier statement as true or made in good faith, still to find qualification at the relevant time. The plaintiff retains the ordinary qualification burden; good faith alone, a bare contradiction or an unexplained statutory label does not satisfy it.

**Authority by component:**

- Cleveland v. Policy Management Systems Corp. — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “SSDI does not create an automatic bar or special adverse presumption under the ADA”, 1999-05-24; Stevens, all nine Justices. “An apparent inconsistency still requires an adequate explanation” supplies the reasonable-juror explanation requirement and ordinary burden.

**Present operation effective:** Cleveland, May 24, 1999.

**Exceptions and limits:** The explanation must address material factual inconsistency, including relevant time, functions and accommodation. A sufficient explanation guarantees neither trial nor success. General judicial-estoppel law, purely factual contradictions, benefits awards and other statutory relationships remain undisturbed.

**Holdings navigation:** [Cleveland v. Policy Management Systems Corp. — SSDI does not create an automatic bar or special adverse presumption under the ADA](HOLDINGS.md#ssdi-does-not-create-an-automatic-bar-or-special-adverse-presumption-under-the-ada-1); [Cleveland v. Policy Management Systems Corp. — An apparent inconsistency still requires an adequate explanation](HOLDINGS.md#an-apparent-inconsistency-still-requires-an-adequate-explanation).

### Written participation in ADEA collective actions

**Governing question:** When an employee becomes a party plaintiff in an ADEA collective action.

**Current rule:** Section 626(b)’s incorporation of §216(b) requires the employee’s written consent before that employee becomes a party plaintiff to an ADEA collective action. Shared policy interests or an opt-out-class analogy cannot replace affirmative written participation. This condition does not make written consent necessary for every independently recognized, constitutionally sufficient form of nonparty binding.

**Authority by component:**

- American Airlines, Inc. v. Tice — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “ADEA collective-action participation”, 1999-06-10; the eight Associate Justices.

**Present operation effective:** Tice, June 10, 1999.

**Holdings navigation:** [American Airlines, Inc. v. Tice — ADEA collective-action participation](HOLDINGS.md#adea-collective-action-participation-1).

### Federal employee representation in agency Inspector General examinations

**Governing question:** When §7114(a)(2)(B) applies to an agency OIG examination and what assistance it permits.

**Current rule:** An agency OIG investigator is an agency representative in an agency-related examination of a covered unit employee when the employee reasonably believes discipline may result and requests representation. OIG independence from ordinary management and exclusion of investigators from bargaining-unit membership do not remove that examination from §7114(a)(2)(B). The exclusive representative may assist but may not obstruct questioning, compromise protected information, direct the investigation or demand bargaining; the investigator may insist on the employee’s own account. Those limits do not justify reducing lawful assistance to silent observation.

**Authority by component:**

- NASA v. FLRA — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “This OIG examination is covered by the statutory representation right”, 1999-06-17; Breyer Part I with Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg. Supplies coverage, predicates and assistance limits.
- NASA v. FLRA — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “Headquarters may be directed to secure this limited statutory compliance”, 1999-06-17; Breyer Part II with Stevens, Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg. Supplies the independently justified headquarters compliance direction, with Stone-Zsela joining that judgment only.

**Present operation effective:** NASA, June 17, 1999.

**Sequence or decisionmaker:** Under retained general supervision, headquarters may direct compliance with this limited statutory right without controlling investigative subjects, evidence, conclusions or termination or bargaining for expanded control.

**Open question:** Outside-agency and FBI examinations, wider criminal or national-security settings, negotiated expansions and a universal interview protocol remain unresolved.

**Holdings navigation:** [National Aeronautics and Space Administration v. Federal Labor Relations Authority — This OIG examination is covered by the statutory representation right](HOLDINGS.md#this-oig-examination-is-covered-by-the-statutory-representation-right-1); [National Aeronautics and Space Administration v. Federal Labor Relations Authority — Headquarters may be directed to secure this limited statutory compliance](HOLDINGS.md#headquarters-may-be-directed-to-secure-this-limited-statutory-compliance).

### Federal driving standards and experimental ADA waivers

**Governing question:** Whether the ADA requires accepting an experimental waiver instead of an otherwise applicable substantive federal vision criterion.

**Current rule:** Where the federal commercial-driving vision criterion remains substantive and the waiver program is an experiment collecting evidence for possible revision, the ADA permits an employer to insist on the ordinary criterion rather than participate in that experiment. The employer need not justify the Government’s standard afresh or independently prove direct threat merely to invoke that program-specific entitlement. Experimental permission is not a completed determination that the substantive criterion has become unnecessary.

**Authority by component:**

- Albertson’s, Inc. v. Kirkingburg — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “The experimental waiver did not require the employer to abandon the ordinary federal vision standard”, 1999-06-22; Kennedy Part I, all nine Justices. The following holding, “Reliance on this federal criterion does not require an independent direct-threat finding”, supplies the bounded defense clarification.

**Present operation effective:** Albertson’s, June 22, 1999.

**Exceptions and limits:** No general license to disregard substantive federal exemptions, mandatory exclusion of waiver holders, unsafe-driving finding or approval of unsupported private standards follows. A regulation making an exemption equivalent to ordinary qualification and other waiver systems remain unresolved. The nonessential disability-method discussion supplies no natural-compensation rule.

**Holdings navigation:** [Albertson’s, Inc. v. Kirkingburg — The experimental waiver did not require the employer to abandon the ordinary federal vision standard](HOLDINGS.md#the-experimental-waiver-did-not-require-the-employer-to-abandon-the-ordinary-federal-vision-standard-1); [Albertson’s, Inc. v. Kirkingburg — Reliance on this federal criterion does not require an independent direct-threat finding](HOLDINGS.md#reliance-on-this-federal-criterion-does-not-require-an-independent-direct-threat-finding).

### Perceived occupational breadth under the original ADA

**Governing question:** What perceived limitation supports a regarded-as-working claim.

**Current rule:** On a working theory under the original ADA, the employer must perceive restriction in a class of jobs or broad range of jobs in various classes relative to comparable training, skills and abilities and the reasonably accessible geographic area. Knowledge of an impairment, rejection from one particular position or a specialized job category, and a claimed regulatory motive do not alone resolve the inquiry. Complete unemployability, exclusion from every position in a vocation or a prescribed percentage is unnecessary. Actual other employment and nationwide reach of a certification rule do not conclusively establish the employer’s perception.

**Authority by component:**

- Murphy v. United Parcel Service, Inc. — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “Regarded-as coverage requires a perceived substantial occupational limitation”, 1999-06-22; Part II-A, all nine Justices. Supplies the perceived-class framework on the assumed regulatory definitions.
- Sutton v. United Air Lines, Inc. — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “Holding 3 — The alleged perceived restriction is confined to a specialized job category”, 1999-06-22; Stone-Zsela Part III, all nine Justices. Supplies the specialized-category limit while assuming working is a major life activity.

**Present operation effective:** Murphy and Sutton, June 22, 1999.

**Open question:** Whether working invariably is a major life activity and the general validity or deference owed all EEOC definitions remain unresolved. Coverage supplies no qualification, business-necessity or direct-threat finding.

**Holdings navigation:** [Murphy v. United Parcel Service, Inc. — Regarded-as coverage requires a perceived substantial occupational limitation](HOLDINGS.md#regarded-as-coverage-requires-a-perceived-substantial-occupational-limitation); [Sutton v. United Air Lines, Inc. — Holding 3 — The alleged perceived restriction is confined to a specialized job category](HOLDINGS.md#holding-3--the-alleged-perceived-restriction-is-confined-to-a-specialized-job-category).

## Bankruptcy

### Ordinary-course eligibility of payments on long-term debt

**Governing question:** Whether debt maturity categorically excludes a payment from the contemporaneous §547(c)(2) preference exception.

**Current rule:** Payments on long-term debt may qualify; maturity supplies no additional categorical exclusion or presumption of ordinariness. The creditor bears §547(g)'s burden to prove all three then-current elements: the debt was incurred in the ordinary course of both parties, payment occurred in their ordinary course, and payment accorded with ordinary business terms. Eligibility alone does not establish any element or exempt all interest or commitment fees.

**Authority by component:**

- Long-term-debt eligibility and all retained statutory elements and burden: Union Bank v. Wolas — Law of the decision, Holding and operative rule, December 11, 1991; Stevens's unanimous opinion.

**Present operation effective:** *Wolas*, December 11, 1991.

**Holdings navigation:** Union Bank v. Wolas, 502 U.S. 151 (1991) — Ordinary-course preference exception.

### Chapter 7 strip-down of allowed real-property liens under §506(d)

**Governing question:** Whether §506(d) reduces an allowed, lien-backed real-property debt to its current judicially determined collateral value in the Chapter 7 setting decided in *Dewsnup*.

**Current rule:** When the claim is allowed under §502 and secured by the real-property lien, §506(d) does not strip that lien down merely because §506(a) values the collateral below the allowed debt. Section 506(a) continues to value secured and unsecured amounts for treatment of the claim; that valuation does not automatically avoid the corresponding lien under §506(d). The rule distinguishes personal discharge from lien survival and does not immunize liens from an independently applicable express avoidance provision.

**Authority by component:**

- Limited Chapter 7 construction and continued valuation function: Dewsnup v. Timm — Allowed real-property liens in the presented Chapter 7 setting, January 15, 1992; Blackmun's opinion joined by White, Stevens, O'Connor, and Kennedy.

**Present operation effective:** *Dewsnup*, January 15, 1992.

**Open question:** Other statutory settings, reorganization restrictions, express statutory exceptions, and estate-administration issues are not resolved by this construction. It does not adopt an abandonment rationale.

**Holdings navigation:** Dewsnup v. Timm, 502 U.S. 410 (1992) — Liens and claim valuation.

### Federal sovereign immunity from affirmative bankruptcy money judgments

**Governing question:** Whether original §106(c), estate-property jurisdiction, or property and trust characterizations authorize an affirmative monetary recovery from the United States under §550.

**Current rule:** Original §106(c) does not unequivocally waive immunity from an affirmative personal money judgment recovering an unauthorized transfer under §550. A plausible reading under which its application-and-binding language governs nonmonetary or claim determinations defeats clear consent to that remedy; legislative history cannot supply missing enacted clarity. Sections 106(a) and (b) retain their own claim-linked and offset operations. General estate-property jurisdiction under §1334(d), an asserted trust interest, and the money's origin in estate assets do not supply the missing consent. An order requiring payment of a sum, rather than adjudicating identified property under the court's control, cannot be preserved by calling it a property proceeding or defensive equitable recoupment.

**Authority by component:**

- Original §106(c) monetary-waiver construction: United States v. Nordic Village — Original §106(c) does not clearly authorize this monetary recovery, February 25, 1992.
- Distinction between jurisdiction and consent; inadequacy of property, trust, and recoupment labels: Nordic Village — Jurisdictional and property labels do not sustain this money judgment, February 25, 1992. Scalia's opinion joined by Stone, White, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, and Thomas controls both.

**Present operation effective:** *Nordic Village*, February 25, 1992.

**Open question:** Genuinely distinct specific-property proceedings require their actual facts and independent authority; their validity is not decided. State immunity and a different express statutory waiver remain outside the decision.

**Holdings navigation:** United States v. Nordic Village, Inc., 503 U.S. 30 (1992) — Federal sovereign immunity.

### Ordinary-check transfer date for preference avoidance

**Governing question:** When an ordinary check transfers the debtor's bank-account interest for the preference period in 11 U.S.C. §547(b).

**Current rule:** The transfer occurs when the drawee honors the ordinary check, because delivery gives the payee no assigned interest in the debtor's account. Section 547(e) does not relate the transfer back to a time before that interest passed. The trustee must still establish the other preference elements, and properly presented statutory defenses retain their separate operation. The construction does not decide transfer timing under §547(c) or for nonordinary payment instruments.

**Authority by component:**
- Honor-date construction and preserved boundaries: Barnhill v. Johnson, March 25, 1992, controlling holding 1, “Honor determines the §547(b) transfer”; Stone for White, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Thomas.

**Present operation effective:** Barnhill, March 25, 1992.

**Holdings navigation:** Barnhill v. Johnson, 503 U.S. 393 (1992) — Preference transfer timing.

### Finality of an unchallenged scheduled exemption

**Governing question:** Whether a trustee may contest a scheduled exemption after the applicable Bankruptcy Rule 4003(b) deadline because the claim lacked a colorable statutory basis.

**Current rule:** Under 11 U.S.C. §522(l) and the applicable Rule 4003(b), property claimed as exempt becomes exempt if no party in interest objects within 30 days after the creditors' meeting concludes or a relevant amendment to the exemption list is filed, whichever is later, and no further time is granted within that period. Rule 9006(b)(3) allows enlargement only on Rule 4003(b)'s conditions. Lack of a colorable substantive exemption supplies no exception permitting a later objection. Uncertainty about a scheduled lawsuit's value permits timely inquiry and objection; it does not require waiting for collection. Properly supported misconduct remedies retain their own conditions and do not supply an adjudicated late-objection exception here.

### Federal-law transfer restrictions and exclusion of trust interests

**Governing question:** Exclusion of a debtor's beneficial trust interest from the estate under 11 U.S.C. §541(c)(2).

**Current rule:** Applicable nonbankruptcy law includes federal law. A transfer restriction on a debtor's beneficial interest in a trust is preserved when enforceable under that law; an established ERISA-qualified trust with an ERISA-enforceable antialienation restriction is therefore excluded from the estate. Exclusion is distinct from exemption and does not change exemption deadlines or adjudicate statutory avoidance remedies.

### Excusable neglect under Rule 9006(b)(1)

**Governing question:** What instructions govern excusable neglect under Rule 9006(b)(1)?

**Current rule:** For a Chapter 11 claim deadline subject to Rule 9006(b)(1), neglect includes inadvertence, mistake and carelessness as well as events beyond control. Post-expiration relief requires a motion and excusability assessed from all relevant circumstances, including debtor prejudice, delay and administrative effects, reason including reasonable control, and good faith. No consideration invariably decides the issue. Freely chosen counsel's conduct is fully attributed to the client; reliance alone is no exception. Under then-effective (b)(2), enlargement is barred for Rules 1007(d), 1017(b)(3), 2003(a) and (d), 7052, 9023 and 9024. Under (b)(3), enlargement is limited to the terms of Rules 1006(b)(2), 1017(e), 3002(c), 4003(b), 4004(a), 4007(c), 8002 and 9033. Thus Chapter 7 claim limits and Taylor's exemption-objection rule gain no general equitable exception.

### Principal-residence mortgage rights in Chapter 13

**Governing question:** What instructions govern principal-residence mortgage rights in Chapter 13?

**Current rule:** When an allowed claim secured only by the debtor's principal-residence real property retains a secured portion, §1322(b)(2) protects the holder's mortgage rights as a whole despite §506(a) valuation and bifurcation. The debtor cannot modify the deficiency portion by altering protected repayment or enforcement rights. Independent restrictions and §1322(b)(5) remain: cure within a reasonable time and maintenance during the case are permitted when the last claim payment falls after the final plan payment, not general rewriting. The stay remains distinct. Wholly unsecured liens and classification of ancillary deed provisions are undecided; Dewsnup's Chapter 7 rule remains separate.

### Oversecured interest and present value of deferred cure arrearages

**Governing question:** What instructions govern oversecured interest and present value of deferred cure arrearages?

**Current rule:** Section 506(b) allows interest on an allowed secured claim within collateral value exceeding the claim after §506(c) recovery, even without contractual arrearage interest; reasonable fees, costs and charges separately require agreement support. Where §1325(a)(5)(B) governs a deferred secured-arrearage cure over creditor objection with retained collateral, lien retention and effective-date present value of at least the allowed claim are required. Section 1322(b)(5)'s cure-and-maintenance authority does not exempt arrearages; acceptance and surrender are separate alternatives. ### Reasonably equivalent value in a forced real-estate sale

**Governing question:** How §548(a)(2) measures value at a mortgage foreclosure.

**Current rule:** Compliance with state foreclosure procedures does not conclusively establish reasonably equivalent value. Compare the price with value under realistically comparable forced-sale conditions, accounting for legally and practically relevant sale constraints. Procedure is relevant evidence, but ordinary open-market appraisal alone is not the comparison and hindsight alone does not establish avoidability. The challenger retains the burden of proving the statutory avoidance predicates, including inadequate value and the independently applicable timing and financial-condition requirements. No mandatory evidence checklist, fixed percentage, categorical price floor or presumption from a low appraisal ratio replaces that inquiry.

**Present operation effective:** BFP v. Resolution Trust Corp, 1994-05-23.

**Open question:** Tax sales, personal-property foreclosures and actual-fraud theories are not resolved. Regular foreclosure is neither a conclusive safe harbor nor automatically avoidable.

### Interim restraint and orderly review in related bankruptcy proceedings

**Governing question:** Collateral displacement of an operative §105 restraint in a proceeding actually related to Chapter 11.

**Current rule:** In a related proceeding supported by an actual bond, retained collateral and reorganization connection, §1334(b) supplies nonexclusive subject-matter jurisdiction; §105 supplies remedial authority, not independent jurisdiction. Section 157(c)(1)’s limit on final noncore adjudication does not eliminate sufficient authority for an interlocutory preservation restraint. Where actual relatedness, sufficient interim authority, substantial support for the applicable restraint and a concrete relief-and-review mechanism are established, a party must challenge it through the issuing proceeding and authorized review rather than execute contrary to it elsewhere while it remains effective.

### Original PLRA nondischargeability of court filing obligations

**Governing question:** The debt category added by §523(a)(17).

**Current rule:** A debt for a court-imposed fee for filing a case, motion, complaint or appeal, or other costs and expenses assessed with respect to that filing, falls within enacted §523(a)(17), regardless of an assertion of poverty under §1915(b) or (f) or prisoner status under §1915(h). The original enacted category is preserved without a later narrowing amendment or an inferred particular discharge decision.

**Authority by component:**

- Added nondischargeability text: PLRA §§802–804 — Source, authority and operative text, §804(b), original 11 U.S.C. §523(a)(17), April 26, 1996.

**Present operation effective:** PLRA, April 26, 1996.

**Effective transition:** The statute was enacted April 26, 1996. Section 802's express all-prospective-relief transition is not generalized to §1997e or §1915; disputed application to pending matters remains unresolved unless an applicable authority separately resolves it.

### Temporary deposit holds pending judicial setoff relief

**Governing question:** Whether preserving a claimed offset through a temporary bank-payment refusal violates the automatic stay.

**Current rule:** A genuinely temporary refusal to pay a deposit debt while promptly seeking judicial setoff relief is not a completed setoff under §362(a)(7) if the creditor has neither intended permanent settlement of the mutual accounts nor finally applied one obligation against the other. Actual legal character governs, not a label or bookkeeping omission. In this deposit-debt setting that temporary preservation also does not violate §362(a)(3)’s control or §362(a)(6)’s collection prohibition. Section 553 preserves qualifying nonbankruptcy rights but creates none; §542(b) excepts payment only to the extent the debt may be offset under §553, and actual offset remains stayed pending lawful relief.

**Authority by component:**

- Strumpf — temporary preservation and distinct control/collection holding, 1995-10-31; Scalia for all nine, Parts I–II.

**Present operation effective:** Strumpf, October 31, 1995.

**Exceptions and limits:** No indefinite freeze, refusal after adverse judicial direction, withholding beyond a legally available offset, general good-faith stay exception or five-day safe harbor follows. The estate’s contractual claim remains estate property. Turnover of other kinds of property, cash collateral, adequate protection and confirmation’s effect retain their distinct rules.

**Holdings navigation:** Citizens Bank of Maryland v. Strumpf, 516 U.S. 16.

### Actual and justifiable reliance for the actual-fraud discharge exception

**Governing question:** Reliance and the extent of nondischargeable liability for an actual-fraud acquisition under §523(a)(2)(A).

**Current rule:** The creditor must prove actual and justifiable reliance by the ordinary preponderance standard. Justifiability depends on that recipient’s knowledge, capacities and circumstances. No universal investigation duty applies, but known or personally obvious falsity defeats justifiability and an actually discovered warning may require inquiry under that individualized standard. Objective imprudence can bear on whether claimed actual reliance occurred, but is not a separate universal prudence condition. Fraud, reliance, justifiability, the obtained-by nexus and the extent of nondischargeable debt remain distinct.

Once money or property is acquired through qualifying §523(a)(2)(A) fraud, the nondischargeable debt includes legally enforceable liability arising from that acquisition, not merely the value received. Connected punitive or treble liability remains included even if wholly punitive, as do valid attributable attorney's fees and costs. State law supplies the underlying liability; federal law supplies discharge treatment. A qualifying federal fraud acquisition and the legal connection remain indispensable: a consumer-fraud label or treble award alone supplies no fraud predicate, and lawful receipts, unrelated obligations and unsupported fee claims remain outside the rule.

Use of a credit card to obtain an advance represents a present intention to repay, not current solvency or an objectively reasonable repayment prospect. On that actual-fraud theory, the creditor must prove by a preponderance that the contemporaneous professed intention was false and deceptive. Financial condition, losses and borrowing patterns may prove state of mind, but inability to pay or unreasonable optimism alone cannot replace the subjective inquiry. The debtor’s denial is not conclusive; no confession, mandatory factor count or additional plan to file bankruptcy is required. Repayment creates no safe harbor for a deliberately false promise.

**Authority by component:**

- Field — Part I, actual and justifiable reliance, 1995-11-28; Souter for all nine, including the two Justices dissenting only from the application and remand.
- Qualifying federal predicate and debt extent: In re Cohen, In re Cohen — I. Federal fraud remains a necessary predicate, In re Cohen — II. The exception covers valid liability for the fraudulent acquisition, In re Cohen — III. The existing treble judgment is nondischargeable even assuming a wholly punitive enhancement and In re Cohen — IV. Existing attributable fees and costs share the debt's treatment; no new award is made, Thomas for all nine, 1997-06-30.

- Credit-card representation and contemporaneous deceptive intent: Canonical Decision Record `att_universal_card_services_v_rembert_merits_1998-12-01.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / Card use communicates an intent to repay, not a warranty of solvency, 1998-12-01; unanimous opinion.

**Present operation effective:** Rembert, 1998-12-01, for the credit-card intent component; Field and In re Cohen retain their earlier component dates.

**Exceptions and limits:** Subsection (A) excludes statements respecting the debtor’s or an insider’s financial condition. Subsection (B) separately requires a materially false written statement of that kind, reasonable creditor reliance and the debtor’s causing publication with intent to deceive. This holding does not separately classify a claim of false pretenses or representation without actual fraud.

**Holdings navigation:** Field v. Mans, 516 U.S. 59. In re Cohen (1997-06-30) — Bankruptcy / Fraud discharge exceptions. [AT&T Universal Card Services v. ### Statutory priorities and claim-specific equitable subordination

**Governing question:** Whether §510(c) permits a court to reduce rank because an allowed penalty competes with compensatory creditors.

**Current rule:** Statutory priority does not immunize a claim from §510(c), and lack of priority does not itself justify subordination. After notice and a hearing, §510(c) permits distributional subordination of all or part of an allowed claim to another allowed claim, or an allowed interest to another allowed interest, under principles of equitable subordination, and transfer of a lien securing a subordinated claim. A legally sufficient, supported claim-specific ground is required; noncompensatory character, estate insufficiency and reduced recovery for innocent or value-giving creditors cannot alone replace Congress’s distribution choices, even when described as individual balancing. This limit applies to both postpetition administrative penalties and prepetition nonpriority penalties.

**Authority by component:**

- Noland — Parts I–II, real statutory equity and forbidden class replacement, 1996-05-13; Thomas for all nine.
- CFI — Part II, the same boundary within the general-unsecured class, 1996-06-20; Souter for all nine.

**Present operation effective:** CFI, June 20, 1996, for application to nonpriority penalties; Noland’s administrative-priority rule effective May 13, 1996.

**Controlling construction:** Allowed §503(b)(1)(C) postpetition tax penalties retain case-era §507(a)(1) priority after conversion through §348(d)’s §503(b) exception. Section 726(a)(4)’s fourth-rank category instead requires a fine, penalty, forfeiture or multiple/exemplary/punitive damages arising before the earlier of the relief order or trustee appointment, and only to the extent noncompensatory. Section 726 distribution remains expressly subject to §510.

**Open question:** Misconduct’s universal necessity remains unresolved; no entitlement without misconduct or frozen catalogue of equitable grounds follows. Rejection of a class-based reason neither orders a new misconduct hearing nor establishes a different ground, final payment or tax priority.

**Holdings navigation:** United States v. Noland, 517 U.S. 535; United States v. Reorganized CF&I Fabricators of Utah, Inc., 518 U.S. 213 (1996).

### Actual statutory operation in bankruptcy tax characterization

**Governing question:** Whether an assessment is a tax entitled to Bankruptcy Code priority.

**Current rule:** Absent an applicable statutory direction adopting an external classification, the exaction’s actual statutory operation controls federal bankruptcy characterization. A tax label and a deterrent purpose are each insufficient alone. The §4971(a) funding-default assessment at issue operates as a noncompensatory penalty because it sanctions failure of an independent pension-funding obligation without satisfying that obligation or replacing pension/PBGC liability; it receives no pre-1994 §507(a)(7)(E) excise-tax priority. The related-penalty route under §507(a)(7)(G) independently requires a qualifying related claim and compensation for actual pecuniary loss. An external provision expressly directing Title 11 tax treatment cannot be disregarded solely because the Bankruptcy Code lacks a reciprocal cross-reference. Section 412(n)(4)(C)’s incorporation of rules similar to ERISA §4068(c), including Title 11 treatment, must be construed with the specified lien conditions and applicable pre-1994 §507(a)(7) requirements before priority is granted. The tax direction concerns an amount with respect to which the specified lien is imposed; the existence and timing of that lien and the effect of the stay remain necessary unresolved predicates in the adjudicated matter.

**Authority by component:**

- CFI — Part I, text-and-operation tax characterization, 1996-06-20; Souter and all participating Justices except Thomas (eight).

- PBGC v. CF&I Fabricators of Utah, Inc. — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “The actual tax-treatment connection must be read with its lien conditions”, 1999-05-13; Souter Parts I and III with Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

**Present operation effective:** PBGC v. CF&I, May 13, 1999, for express external Title 11 incorporation; the separate §4971 assessment rule remains effective June 20, 1996.

**Exceptions and limits:** Minimum-funding waivers can remove the deficiency underlying either the ordinary or additional assessment; the distinction is not a finding that only the additional assessment is avoidable. Congress may expressly assign priority. This supplies no general Lorber checklist, constitutional punishment classification, disallowance, dischargeability determination or independent ground of equitable subordination.

### Replacement valuation for retained Chapter 13 collateral

**Governing question:** Valuation under §§506(a) and 1325(a)(5)(B) when the debtor retains collateral for use.

**Current rule:** Use the price a willing buyer in the debtor's trade, business or situation would pay a willing seller for comparable property of the same age and condition serving the proposed retained use. This is adjusted replacement value, not net foreclosure value for a sale the plan prevents. The court selects appropriate market evidence; it must exclude separately included warranties, storage, reconditioning or other benefits not received through retention, and accessories or modifications outside the creditor's lien cannot enlarge secured value.

**Authority by component:**

- Associates Commercial Corp. v. Rash — Holdings, 1997-06-16; Ginsburg with Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Breyer; eight, holding and operative rule for retained-use replacement valuation

**Present operation effective:** Rash, 1997-06-16.

**Exceptions and limits:** Replacement value is not new-property cost, a mandatory retail quote, debtor-specific earnings or a midpoint between incompatible standards. Appropriate adjustments do not mechanically remove every dealer profit or overhead component from a demonstrated comparable-market price. Surrender, abandonment and materially different uses remain unresolved. No dollar valuation, interest rate, disposition expense or universal rule for other bankruptcy provisions is fixed.

### Enabling-loan perfection within the federal preference period

**Governing question:** The applicable twenty-day perfection condition under §547(c)(3)(B).

**Current rule:** All acts required by state law to perfect a qualifying enabling-loan security interest must be completed within twenty days after the debtor receives possession for the applicable §547(c)(3) exception. A longer state relation-back period cannot turn later completion into timely federal perfection. State law supplies the interest and the acts achieving protection against a simple-contract creditor’s superior judicial lien under §547(e)(1)(B); federal law supplies the deadline. Required governmental acts count when state law makes them necessary; timely creditor effort or mailing alone is no universal safe harbor.

**Authority by component:**

- State-required perfection acts within the federal twenty days: Fidelity Financial Services, Inc. v. Fink, 1998-01-13; Stone-Zsela for all nine Justices.

**Present operation effective:** 1998-01-13.

**Exceptions and limits:** The exception also requires the specified new value under the signed property-describing security agreement, given by or for the secured party to enable acquisition and actually so used. Section 547(b)’s preference predicates remain separate. The rule preserves state creation and priority outside the displaced timing consequence and applies no later amended interval.

**Holdings navigation:** Fidelity Financial Services, Inc. v. Fink — Enabling-loan perfection and preference avoidance.

### Injury-directed intent under the willful-and-malicious discharge exception

**Governing question:** What intent makes an injury willful under 11 U.S.C. §523(a)(6)?

**Current rule:** Willfulness requires intentional injury, not merely an intentional act that causes negligent or reckless harm. The independent maliciousness requirement must also be met. A state tort label, severe malpractice or uninsured practice supplies no substitute for the federal injury-intent predicate; conversion likewise is not automatically a willful and malicious injury.

**Open question:** The independent meaning of maliciousness and whether subjective knowledge of substantial certainty satisfies willfulness remain unresolved; other independently pleaded discharge exceptions retain their own requirements.

**Holdings navigation:** Kawaauhau v. Geiger — Injury-intent discharge exception.

### Consumer collateral retention and reaffirmation approval

**Governing question:** What then-effective §§521(2) and 524 require when an individual consumer debtor proposes to retain collateral.

**Current rule:** Section 521(2) requires the statement of retention or surrender for covered scheduled consumer debts secured by estate property within thirty days after filing or by the creditors’ meeting, whichever is earlier, subject to a for-cause extension fixed within that period. Exemption, redemption or reaffirmation must be specified when applicable. The debtor must perform the lawful stated intention within forty-five days after notice, subject to a for-cause extension fixed within those forty-five days. With subparagraph (C)’s preservation of debtor and trustee rights, those duties do not themselves make surrender, redemption and reaffirmation exclusive substantive options. Continued payment and retention remain permissible insofar as existing law and the enforceable agreement permit; no lien stripping, excuse of lawful default or judicially reduced installment redemption follows.

For an unrepresented individual covered by §524(c)(6)(A), approval independently requires both absence of undue hardship to the debtor or a dependent and the debtor’s best interest. Agreement or signature alone satisfies neither condition. Subsection (6)(B)’s exception concerns consumer debt secured by real property. Voluntary repayment under §524(f) does not restore enforceable discharged personal liability; all other §524(c)–(d) conditions remain.

### Old-equity exclusivity and Chapter 11 absolute priority

**Governing question:** Whether old equity may receive an exclusive new-capital investment opportunity over an unpaid impaired senior class’s objection.

**Current rule:** When an impaired senior unsecured class objects and is not paid in full, §1129(b)(2)(B)(ii) forbids reserving to old equity alone the opportunity to contribute capital and acquire reorganized ownership when old ownership supplies the exclusive eligibility. That opportunity is property received on account of the old interest even if new money purchases new ownership and the valuations are unchallenged. Lawful proposal exclusivity under §1121 does not independently make the resulting ownership preference confirmable.

### Prepetition pension compensation and administrative priority

**Governing question:** Whether later pension-funding dates convert compensation for prepetition service into an administrative debt.

**Current rule:** Pension contributions attributable to prepetition employee services do not receive §503(b)(1)(A) administrative priority merely because payment falls due later, a funding duty continues or the plan later terminates. Compensation for actual postpetition service remains distinct. The debt’s origin must be identified; continued operations do not make every earlier-service obligation newly incurred.
